newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open lower, profit-taking, dlr cited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open lower, profit-taking, dlr cited.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened lower on Friday, pressured by profit-taking and a slightly weaker dollar.
The 6-1/2 percent 30-year bond was down 5/32 to 100-28/32. The benchmark bond yield was up to 6.43 percent, a shade higher than its closing yield on Thursday of 6.42 percent.

The market has several pieces of economic data on its menu. The first of them -- October industrial production and capacity utilization figures from the Federal Reserve -- are expected to be market friendly.

With manufacturing restrained by the now-ended General Motors strike, October industrial production is expected to be unchanged from September, when production rose 0.2 percent over the previous month. The portion of the nation's mines, factories and utilities employed in that production is expected to have fallen to 83.0 percent in October from 83.3 percent in September.

After the 0915 EST/1316 GMT release of the industrial production and capacity use data, the market gets September business inventories figures at 1000 EST/1500 GMT. Forecast at up 0.2 percent, they are not seen as a market mover.

The preliminary November University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey is also due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT. Analysts look for a reading of 95.7, slightly diminished from the final October reading of 96.5.
The profit-taking that weighed on Treasury prices overnight carried over into early trade in New York, an unsurprising phenomenon considering how far the market has advanced, analysts said.
"We're pushing against the envelope in terms of important data events," said William Sullivan, senior vice president and director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter Reynolds.
Sullivan said the industrial production and capacity utiization data should be favorable for the market, with output held in check by the GM strike.

"The month's important statistics are behind us," said Sullivan, predicting that the market could go into "a holding pattern" going through the late November Thanksgiving holiday and "up until the next payroll report." The November payroll employment report is due on Friday, December 6.
Sullivan also said the dollar could be a "marginal influence" as to how the Treasury market trades in November.
Politics and the waxing and waning prospects for a balanced Federal budget will be "a neutral" for the market for the rest of the calendar year, said Sullivan.
"Clinton is going (on a trip) to Asia and (Senate Majority Leader) Trent Lott is setting up an agenda for the GOP-controlled, 105th Congress," Sullivan observed. "Politics will be a wet noodle here."
In early trade, three-month bill rates were down one basis point to 5.02 percent. Six-month and year-bill rates were up one basis point each to 5.07 and 5.12 percent, respectively.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 at 100-12/32 to yield 5.67 percent. Five-year notes were down 3/32 to 101-9/32, yielding 5.95 percent. Ten-year notes were down 5/32 to 102-13/32, yielding 6.17 percent.
